cards.title: Lars and Jens Rasmussen
cards.body: Google took an interest in the Rasmussen brothers' tiny mapping startup Where 2 Tech in early 2004; they joined and helped create Google Maps. They left Maps for a project codenamed Walkabout. A five-person team in Google's Sydney office built the prototype; more than two years later, on 28 May 2009, Lars previewed Google Wave to developers.
cards.prompt: The Wave team's target was not the word processor. What everyday system did they set out to replace, and what was the argument for replacing it?
cards.answer: Email, and instant messaging with it. Jens Rasmussen's argument: both were 1960s designs imitating analog formats — email mimicked snail mail, IM mimicked phone calls — so he proposed one communication model spanning conversation and document, built for what computers and networks could now do.

cards.title: Wave cancelled
cards.body: Urs Hölzle, Senior Vice President of Operations and Google Fellow, posted "Update on Google Wave" on 4 August 2010, fourteen months after the developer preview. It praises the demo that made developers stand and cheer, then closes the product. The announcement named no cost.
cards.prompt: Google gave exactly one reason for cancelling Wave, in one sentence. What was it — and what does it notably not blame?
cards.answer: "Wave has not seen the user adoption we would have liked." It is a demand problem. Nothing in the announcement says the operational transformation, the federation protocol or the engineering failed; Google said it would keep the site up at least through the end of the year and extend the technology into other projects.

cards.title: Google Wave Operational Transformation
cards.body: By David Wang, Alex Mah and Soren Lassen. Wave's concurrency-control design, published the month before Google cancelled the product and still readable in the Apache Wave repository, next to the federation whitepaper that says which server does the transforming.
cards.prompt: Wave's OT whitepaper changes one thing about textbook OT so the server stays cheap. What must the client do, what does the server then need only one of, and which 1995 system is the starting point?
cards.answer: The client must wait for the server's acknowledgement before sending more operations, composing its pending edits meanwhile. The server then needs only a single state space — the history of operations it has applied — instead of one per connected client. The starting point is the Jupiter collaboration system paper of 1995.

cards.title: The sequencer everybody kept
cards.body: Same company, same year: on 15 April 2010, months before Wave was cancelled, Google Docs released a preview of a rebuilt editor in which collaborators' keystrokes appear character-by-character. Hosted, never federated — and nobody asked it to be.
cards.prompt: Wave was cancelled but its code was not deleted. Where did it go, when did that end, and which line of research took over the job of removing the central server?
cards.answer: The Apache Incubator: Wave entered incubation on 1 December 2010 and the podling retired on 15 January 2018 — it never graduated, so it is not in the Apache Attic. The work of removing the central server moved into CRDT research, which buys it by giving every character a permanent identity: metadata and tombstones that never shrink.
